title: Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation

concept.text: The innovation would be a programmable quantum computer that keeps errors under control throughout a large, useful computation. It would combine many imperfect physical qubits into protected logical qubits, perform a universal set of logical operations, and run an application whose scale and reliability make it consequential—for example, cryptographic-size integer factoring or a scientifically useful quantum simulation with a persuasive advantage over classical methods.

Fault-tolerance theorems explain how reliable quantum computation can be possible under specified noise, locality, and architectural assumptions when physical errors are sufficiently weak. Turning that possibility into a machine requires more than preserving a quantum state: error correction, logical gates, decoding, classical control, and application execution must work together for the full computation. Protected memories and small logical circuits are milestones within this concept, rather than separate realizations of the application-scale goal.

significance.text: A successful machine would add a major computational capability to the existing digital-computing toolkit. Shor’s algorithms establish polynomial-time quantum methods for integer factoring and specified discrete-logarithm problems. Executing these methods at cryptographically relevant sizes would threaten RSA and other public-key cryptosystems whose security depends on the affected mathematical problems, wherever those systems remained deployed without adequate post-quantum protection. This is a concrete algorithmic consequence; it does not depend on quantum computers accelerating every kind of computation.

Quantum simulation offers another consequential application, particularly for selected quantum dynamics that are difficult to reproduce classically. Reliable application-scale computation could make some otherwise inaccessible physical predictions practical. Drug, battery, and materials discovery are conditional downstream possibilities: they additionally require suitable algorithms, tractable state preparation, informative measurements, relevant chemical models, and experimental validation. Neither universal programmability nor error correction establishes efficient solutions for every quantum-system problem, including difficult ground-state problems.

General logistics optimization and efficient solutions to NP-complete problems do not follow from this capability. Grover’s algorithm provides a quadratic improvement in exhaustive search, which can still leave an exponentially growing workload. The supplied perspective describes continuing uncertainty about useful quantum optimization advantages and does not establish polynomial-time quantum algorithms for NP-complete problems. These limits matter when translating a specific quantum advantage into claims about broad economic impact.

Interpretive synthesis: a checked application-scale quantum advantage would provide empirical evidence that quantum hardware can outperform practical classical competitors on a consequential task. A finite demonstration would not prove an asymptotic separation from every possible classical algorithm or a general impossibility of efficient classical simulation. Computation beyond the quantum model would require a separate physical and computational justification; it is not a consequence of fault tolerance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is sustained, universal logical computation at an application scale, with a sufficiently low total failure probability and acceptable resource cost. A memory experiment tests whether encoded information survives. An application also requires reliable operations on that information, including the ingredients needed beyond Clifford circuits, while repeated measurements, decoding, and control continue throughout the run. Quantinuum’s supplied report identifies magic-state preparation and integrated real-time decoding among the remaining steps toward universal circuits.

The engineering challenge is to preserve error suppression as the machine grows and performs a much larger workload. Physical noise must remain compatible with the assumptions underlying the chosen code and architecture; logical gates must be protected alongside storage; and classical decoding and control must respond quickly enough to support the computation. A low error rate in a small code or an offline decoding analysis does not by itself establish these capabilities in an integrated machine.

Resource overhead remains a concrete barrier. Physical qubits are the noisy hardware elements; logical qubits are the protected computational units built from them. Gidney’s RSA-2048 estimate concerns fewer than one million noisy physical qubits, not millions of logical qubits. Its feasibility depends on hardware timing, connectivity, noise, algorithmic choices, and storage behavior. Achieving an attractive projected qubit count therefore requires realizing the model’s operating assumptions, rather than merely manufacturing that number of qubits.

Useful application execution also requires credible validation and classical comparison. Factoring has an easily checked output because the proposed factors can be multiplied. A large quantum simulation can be harder to verify: agreement with experiments, known limits, or smaller exactly solvable cases contributes evidence, but does not alone certify an answer in a larger classically inaccessible regime. Application value depends on the complete preparation, computation, measurement, and validation process, alongside the strength of competing classical methods.

current_state.text: Eisert and Preskill’s assessment, first submitted in October 2025 and revised on 21 May 2026, describes substantial gaps between noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices and application-scale fault-tolerant machines. It distinguishes extended quantum memories from the subsequent realization of universal computers that solve hard problems. The demonstrations covered by the supplied review do not establish cryptographic-size Shor execution or a universal application-scale machine. Because the supplied freshness record is empty, this is a conclusion about the reviewed sources, not an exhaustive survey through 1 November 2026.

Google’s Willow experiment, published online on 9 December 2024 and appearing in Nature in 2025, reports a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory with an error rate of 0.143% ± 0.003 percentage points per correction cycle and a lifetime beyond breakeven. Integrated real-time decoding was demonstrated separately at distance 5; it should not be attributed to the distance-7 result. The retrieved main article records an author correction dated 28 April 2026. The supplied review did not inspect the separate correction text or establish its precise effects, so these figures retain that qualification. Supplementary artifacts in the source index do not extend the review’s stated inspection scope.

Quantinuum’s Helios preprint, submitted on 16 October 2026, reports color-code memories at distances 3, 5, and 7, together with below-threshold two-qubit Clifford benchmarking at distances 3 and 5. Its estimated distance-7 memory error rate is approximately 5×10^-6 per syndrome-extraction cycle, with a reported interval of 3×10^-6 to 9×10^-6. The estimate comes from three failures in 29,000 shots, each lasting 20 cycles, making the finite-shot uncertainty important to interpretation. This is a preprint report of small encoded memories and circuits, rather than an application-scale universal computation.

All decoding in the Quantinuum experiment was performed offline. Decoder timing studies indicate potential for real-time integration, but do not constitute an integrated real-time demonstration. Its memory error rate and Google’s rate also come from different codes and experimental protocols; the supplied review does not establish a controlled comparison between the platforms. The results demonstrate progress in error correction without resolving the remaining universal-gate, control, and application-scaling requirements.

Gidney’s May 2025 analysis estimates RSA-2048 factoring in under a week with fewer than one million noisy physical qubits; the reviewed resource accounting gives a total of 897,864 physical qubits. This is a planning estimate, not a hardware demonstration. It assumes a square nearest-neighbor grid, uniform 0.1% gate errors, a 1-microsecond surface-code cycle, and a 10-microsecond control reaction time, alongside algorithmic and implementation assumptions. The review also identifies conjectural algorithmic assumptions and unfinished detailed analysis and simulation of cold-storage behavior under different workloads. The numerical estimate must be interpreted within those conditions.

The historical threshold theorem supplies a foundation for these efforts rather than evidence of a completed machine. The supplied review inspected its opening discussion of locality and reliable universal computation, but the retained PDF extraction is truncated on page 39. That limitation does not negate the supported theorem-to-machine distinction; it limits claims about coverage of the complete technical treatment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed sufficient cryptanalytic milestone: factor an independently selected public RSA modulus of at least 2048 bits, constructed from two comparably sized primes, with its factors unavailable to the implementers beforehand. Use Shor’s algorithm or an equivalent peer-reviewed quantum cryptanalytic algorithm, execute fault-tolerant logical operations with ongoing error correction, and verify the factors classically. A circuit whose construction already uses the factors would not qualify. The 2048-bit threshold is a proposed criterion for this record, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Classically verified fault-tolerant factoring of unknown ≥2048-bit RSA modulus

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence requirements: publish the computation protocol, circuit-generation procedure, physical and logical resource counts, decoding and control methods, run records, success statistics, and end-to-end elapsed time. Compare the result with credible classical methods on the same task, including relevant preparation and processing costs. Make enough information available for independent scrutiny and replication, and repeat the demonstration on independently selected inputs so that a single favorable instance does not carry the whole claim.
completion_criteria.label: Published records and independent replications versus credible classical methods

completion_criteria.text: Proposed universality requirement: establish programmable execution of a universal logical gate set separately from the factoring result, including the operations beyond the demonstrated Clifford circuits and their integration with real-time correction and control. Protected memory, sampling, or one specialized application alone would not establish unrestricted programmability. Finite tests could demonstrate a stated breadth of programs, scales, and operating conditions; they could not establish literal universality by exhaustive testing.
completion_criteria.label: Programmable universal logical gates beyond Clifford with real-time correction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed alternative application milestone: execute a scientifically useful quantum simulation at a scale where the complete computation offers a persuasive accuracy or time advantage over strong classical methods. Specify the physical question, error tolerance, state-preparation and measurement costs, and a validation strategy suitable for the otherwise inaccessible regime. Smaller exact cases and experimental agreement should contribute to that strategy without being presented as complete verification of the larger answer. This preserves the broader concept rather than making cryptanalysis its exclusive completion route.
completion_criteria.label: Useful quantum simulation with persuasive advantage over strong classical methods

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the demonstrated workload size, runtime, failure probability, calibration demands, and hardware and classical-computing requirements. A convincing application-scale demonstration need not establish commercial value in every domain or efficient solutions to arbitrary computational problems. Its claim should remain bounded by the applications and operating conditions actually demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Reported practical bounds on workload, reliability, and computing requirements

related_concepts.text: CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, concerns a different computational breakthrough. Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing would implement known quantum capabilities, while Grover’s quadratic search advantage does not supply polynomial-time solutions to NP-complete problems. The roster provides CSC-01’s title but no detailed definition, so a more specific boundary cannot be assessed.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation, share a cryptographic context with this entry but concern different capabilities. They address computation while protecting information or program details; this entry concerns reliable execution of quantum algorithms, including algorithms that threaten particular cryptographic assumptions. The supplied titles do not establish that either privacy technology is automatically defeated or enabled by this machine.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software; CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery; and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, overlap with the demand for trustworthy computational results. Their central goals concern proofs, discovery, or behavioral guarantees. Fault-tolerant quantum computation instead protects a physical computation against errors. Classical verification of factors is useful evidence for a quantum run, but it does not itself deliver any of those broader verification capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence; CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems; and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, concern intelligence, learning theory, and embodied action. Quantum hardware might eventually serve particular subroutines within such systems, but the supplied material establishes no dependency or automatic route from quantum fault tolerance to these outcomes. They remain distinct entries.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty, so comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 remains unestablished.
The separate Google author correction dated 28 April 2026 was not inspected in the supplied review; its precise changes and any effects on the stated results remain unresolved.
Quantinuum’s October 2026 findings are preprint reports in this packet. Independent replication and subsequent peer-reviewed disposition are not established here.

The precise Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani random-oracle lower bound cannot be verified from the packet because the cited zbMATH source has no retained artifact. Its omission is an evidence limitation, not a finding that the theorem is false.
The original elliptic-curve-specific cryptanalytic assertion is not established by the inspected Shor paper; resolving that attribution would require evidence outside this packet.
Gidney’s estimate retains conjectural algorithmic assumptions and unfinished cold-storage workload analysis; the packet does not resolve their effect on realizable resources and runtime.
A concrete validation protocol for a classically inaccessible application-scale simulation remains application dependent and is not specified by the supplied sources.
Related-concept boundaries beyond the supplied roster titles remain provisional because full definitions of the other entries were not provided.

The research mentions Preskill’s February 2025 Megaquop perspective, but the supplied source index and validated review do not document its inspection. Its historical statement about commercially valuable NISQ advantage was not promoted into an independently reviewed current-state claim.

brief.title: Quantum computers that finish large, useful calculations
possible: Scientists could calculate how selected quantum systems behave where ordinary computers struggle. Cryptographers could split large numbers used in encryption into their prime factors. A programmable quantum computer would keep errors under control throughout these long calculations.
The machine would combine imperfect qubits, the hardware units of quantum information, into protected logical qubits. It would preserve that protection while carrying out useful programs.
why: Reliable quantum simulation could give scientists access to physical predictions that are otherwise out of reach.

Large-scale factoring would threaten RSA, an encryption system whose security depends on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. Systems still using vulnerable encryption would need protection designed to withstand quantum attacks.

shown: Google has kept protected quantum information alive longer than its best constituent qubit. Quantinuum reports protection that improves with scale in memories and limited circuits. Its result is a preprint, and its smallest error estimate rests on few observed failures.

Error interpretation and control must keep pace while protection survives a much larger workload.
A complete application must deliver a credible advantage over strong ordinary-computer methods at an acceptable resource cost.

milestones.label: Checked factors of an independently selected encryption number
milestones.explanation: A protected quantum computation would have to factor an independently selected RSA number of at least 2048 binary digits without knowing its factors beforehand. Ordinary multiplication would check the cryptanalytic result.

milestones.label: Published results that independent teams can repeat
milestones.explanation: Public methods, resources, timings and success records would have to support independent replication across independently selected inputs and fair classical comparisons. This would establish that the advantage survives scrutiny.

milestones.label: A full range of programmable protected operations
milestones.explanation: Separate tests would have to demonstrate a programmable, complete set of protected operations with error correction and control during execution. This would establish broader capability than memory or a specialized calculation.

milestones.label: Useful simulation with a persuasive computing advantage
milestones.explanation: A scientifically useful quantum simulation would have to beat strong classical methods after preparation and measurement costs, with a credible validation strategy. This would provide an alternative application milestone to factoring.

milestones.label: Measured limits on workload, reliability and resources
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would have to report workload, runtime, failure probability, calibration needs and quantum and classical computing requirements. These measurements would establish the practical boundaries of its capability.

uncertain: How well will error suppression survive larger machines and longer computations?
How can scientists validate a simulation answer beyond the reach of ordinary computers?
The proposed factoring size is a milestone criterion, rather than an agreed standard; projected resources also depend on unresolved assumptions.

page.title: Utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation
page.definition: A programmable quantum computer runs application workloads while correcting errors in logical qubits, quantum information encoded across physical qubits. Its protected gates can approximate arbitrary quantum circuits; utility scale uses DARPA's test that computational value exceeds lifetime acquisition, operating and maintenance costs.

goal.need: Shor's algorithm factors integers in a number of steps polynomial in their bit length, making RSA factoring a concrete application. Gidney's RSA-2048 estimate assumes a square nearest-neighbour layout, 0.1% gate errors, 1 μs error-correction cycles and 10 μs control response. The resource requirements below are a preprint estimate, not an executed cryptanalytic calculation.

figures.caption: Gidney's estimated resources for fault-tolerant RSA factoring
figures.note: Conditional resource estimate from a preprint; operating assumptions are stated above.

completion.title: A universal fault-tolerant quantum computer delivers computational value greater than its lifetime cost.
completion.criterion: An operating programmable computer with a universal set of fault-tolerant logical gates delivers computational value greater than its cost: value/cost > 1. DARPA's QBI measures value in dollars and includes the customer's acquisition, operating and maintenance expenses over a reasonable system lifetime; preceding R&D is excluded. The valuation is application- and system-specific. A validated construction plan alone does not establish operation.
completion.set_by: DARPA, QBI solicitation DARPA-PS-24-26, section II.B.3 and footnote 4, with valuation clarified in Q&A 8. Universal logical gates follow the field convention exemplified by Postler et al.
completion.threshold_quote: one whose computational value exceeds its costs
completion.basis: The universal logical-gate requirement defines the computing capability. DARPA's qualitative value-over-cost definition supplies the application-scale test without imposing an arbitrary factoring size or qubit count. QBI Stage C assesses readiness for construction, which precedes demonstrating this criterion in an operating system.

milestones.title: An error-corrected logical qubit outlives its best constituent physical qubit.
milestones.criterion: The logical storage lifetime exceeds that of the best constituent physical qubit under the comparison protocol. On 9 December 2024, Google reported a 101-physical-qubit, distance-7 memory with lifetime ratio 2.4 ± 0.3. The correction published on 28 April 2026 amends repetition-code figure labels.
milestones.set_by: Quantum-error-correction community's memory breakeven convention, explicitly applied by Google Quantum AI; the cited experiment used superconducting circuits.
milestones.threshold_quote: exceeding the lifetime of its best physical qubit

milestones.title: Increasing code distance suppresses encoded errors exponentially, with suppression factor Λ > 1.
milestones.criterion: At comparable physical noise, increasing code distance reduces logical errors exponentially; fitted suppression Λ exceeds 1. Code distance is the minimum weight of a nontrivial logical Pauli operator. Google reported Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 for distances 3, 5 and 7 on 9 December 2024. Quantinuum's preprint of 16 October 2026 reports distance-7 memory error 5 (+4/−2) × 10⁻⁶ per cycle from 3 failures in 29,000 shots of 20 cycles; two-qubit Clifford tests used distances 3 and 5, with all decoding offline. Arrays of up to 448 neutral atoms gave Λ = 2.14 ± 0.13 over four correction rounds, published on 10 November 2025.
milestones.set_by: Quantum-error-correction community's below-threshold scaling criterion, applied in the cited superconducting, trapped-ion and neutral-atom experiments.
milestones.threshold_quote: suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold.

milestones.title: A processor executes a fault-tolerant universal gate set on logical qubits.
milestones.criterion: Execute logical one-qubit and entangling operations forming a universal gate set, with fault-tolerant constructions that prevent correctable faults spreading into uncorrectable errors. Universality permits arbitrary quantum circuits to be approximated to arbitrary accuracy. On 25 May 2022, Postler et al. reported two encoded trapped-ion qubits, a logical controlled-NOT and magic-state-injected T gate. Bluvstein et al. demonstrated neutral-atom universal-logic ingredients using [[15,1,3]] code blocks, published on 10 November 2025.
milestones.set_by: Quantum-computing community's universal fault-tolerant gate-set criterion; Postler et al. apply it to two trapped-ion logical qubits.
milestones.threshold_quote: a fault-tolerant universal set of gates on two logical qubits

milestones.title: A decoder keeps pace with error correction and supplies corrections before dependent logical gates.
milestones.criterion: The integrated decoder processes error syndromes at their production rate, or close enough to avoid exponential backlog, and returns corrections before dependent logical operations. Throughput and response latency are separate requirements. Google's report of 9 December 2024 tested a distance-5 memory on 72 physical qubits for up to 10⁶ cycles: mean decoder latency was 63 ± 17 μs, with ten shots per duration. Feedback was not implemented, so this establishes memory throughput rather than the complete gate-feedback requirement.
milestones.set_by: Real-time-decoding requirements published by Battistel et al. in Nano Futures; timing requirements depend on the hardware platform.
milestones.threshold_quote: the decoder needs to process the syndrome data at the same rate as it is received or close to it

milestones.title: An error-corrected processor executes circuits containing about one million logical operations.
milestones.criterion: Execute circuits with roughly 10⁶ quantum operations on protected logical qubits. Preskill's megaquop regime is explicitly approximate. His example of order 100 logical qubits and depth 10,000 is illustrative, and his order-10⁻⁶ error per logical gate is a heuristic rather than an acceptance limit. QuEra's roadmap adopts the megaquop designation for Libra. None of the cited experimental results establishes this circuit workload.
milestones.set_by: Preskill's published megaquop convention, also adopted in QuEra's roadmap; this is an approximate named regime rather than a formal standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: mega means not precisely a million but somewhere in the vicinity of a million.

milestones.title: Hardware prototypes pass DARPA's readiness test for constructing a utility-scale quantum computer.
milestones.criterion: Components and major hardware prototypes pass DARPA's system-specific evaluation, and DARPA judges the approach ready to begin final design and construction of a utility-scale system. This requires successful completion of QBI Stage C. DARPA's list current on 8 October 2026 places Atom Computing, Diraq, IBM, IonQ, Microsoft and PsiQuantum in active Stage C; admission to Stage C does not satisfy this milestone.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, QBI Stage C completion criterion, published in its solicitation and Proposers Day presentation of 3 September 2024.
milestones.threshold_quote:
ready to immediately begin the final design and
construction of a USQC whose value exceeds its cost

results.finding: A 101-physical-qubit logical memory outlived its best constituent physical qubit by 2.4 ± 0.3 times.
results.detail: The distance-7 logical lifetime was compared with constituent physical-qubit lifetimes using a uniform average over pure states.
results.quote: The distance-7 logical qubit lifetime is 291 ± 6 μs, exceeding the lifetimes of all the constituent physical qubits (median, 85 ± 7 μs; best, 119 ± 13 μs) by a factor of 2.4 ± 0.3.

results.finding: Surface-code memories at distances 3, 5 and 7 achieved a fitted suppression factor Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02.
results.detail: The comparison averaged nine distance-3 and four distance-5 subgrids against one distance-7 code; decoding was offline.
results.quote:
With our neural network decoder, we observe
Λ

results.finding: A 72-qubit distance-5 memory had mean decoder latency of 63 ± 17 μs over experiments up to one million cycles.
results.detail: Latency stayed approximately constant as experiment duration increased, indicating sustained decoding throughput. Ten shots were measured per duration; feedback before dependent logical gates was not implemented.
results.quote: We observe that the average decoder latency remains roughly constant at a net average of 63 ± 17 μs independent of the length of the experiment (up to 1.1 s), indicating that the decoding problem is being processed in real time.

results.finding: Color-code memory experiments across 66,440 shots at distances 3, 5 and 7 yielded a fitted suppression factor Λ = 12 (+3/−2).
results.detail: Each shot used 20 correction cycles. The distance-7 estimate came from 3 failures in 29,000 shots; decoding was offline.
results.quote:
Leveraging both circuit- and hardware-
level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as 5+4−2 ×10 −6, and demonstrate
error suppression by over an order of magnitude, Λ = 12 +3−2, with each successive increase in code
distance.

results.finding: Encoded two-qubit Clifford benchmarking sampled 3,996 circuits; distance-5 error was 7 (+3/−3) × 10⁻⁵ per Clifford.
results.detail: The experiments used transversal logical Clifford gates, including entangling gates. They did not demonstrate a non-Clifford T gate or a universal gate set.
results.quote:
This work demonstrates high accuracy,
below threshold implementation of the last two compo-
nents on an ion-trap device.

results.finding: Streaming decoders processed 66,440 previously acquired records; the distance-7 transformer averaged 0.35 ms per round.
results.detail: Decoding was offline. Neural-network timings were GPU compute times; the Frontier timing test ran on a laptop and excluded control-stack overhead. Corrections were not supplied before dependent gates.
results.quote:
All three streaming decoders support processing syn-
drome data as they arrive. Therefore, while all decod-
ing in this work has been done offline, the syndromes
have been fed to the streaming decoders one round at
a time to study their processing time that is relevant
for real time decoding.

results.finding: Trapped-ion logical memory using 10 data qubits achieved approximately 10× the physical-layer lifetime by process fidelity.
results.detail: The physical-qubit measurements were averaged across trap regions; the text does not establish a comparison against the best constituent physical qubit. The 1/e lifetime ratio is model-fitted and may not apply in the small-error regime.
results.quote: Our results show over an order-of-magnitude improvement in the lifetime of the encoded qubit over the physical layer qubit

results.finding: Neutral-atom distance-7 repetition-code logical memory: 225 ± 33 s lifetime; number of experimental shots not reported.
results.detail: The fitted logical lifetime exceeded the longer measured idle-atom survival lifetime of 15.6 ± 0.5 s. The phase-sensitive memory used repeated error correction, atom replacement and reservoir refilling; the physical baseline measured atom survival.
results.quote: Using a repetition code of distance 3 or 7 to periodically correct for errors occurring in interleaved wait-times, we show that logical information decays on a timescale of over 3 minutes for the larger distance, even when underlying qubits have lifetimes in the system on the order of 10 seconds.

results.finding: Neutral-atom arrays of up to 448 atoms: logical-error suppression factor Λ = 2.14 ± 0.13.
results.detail: Distance 5 was compared with distance 3 over four correction rounds, using loss information and machine-learning decoding without postselection.
results.quote:

results.finding: A trapped-ion processor demonstrated a fault-tolerant universal gate set on 2 logical qubits.
results.detail: The demonstration included a logical controlled-NOT and a logical T gate injected using a fault-tolerantly prepared magic state.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate a fault-tolerant universal set of gates on two logical qubits in a trapped-ion quantum computer.

results.finding: Trapped-ion processor realized a fault-tolerant universal gate set on 3 logical qubits; tomography used 7,500 shots per state, qubit and basis.
results.detail: The [[8,3,2]] code detects single errors; results used postselection. The universal set combines a logical Hadamard, CNOT and CCZ.
results.quote: Moreover, we realize a fault-tolerant universal gate set on an eight-qubit error-detecting code hosting three logical qubits, based on state injection, which can be executed by coherent gate operations only.

results.finding: On a 20-qubit trapped-ion processor, researchers benchmarked a fault-tolerant logical controlled-Hadamard gate on two encoded qubits.
results.detail: The experiment also benchmarked a logical single-qubit rotation, but the text does not establish that the demonstrated operations form a universal gate set. The experiments used a distance-2 error-detecting code and post-selection; the higher-distance protocol was simulated.
results.quote: We experimentally benchmark this eight qubit magic state preparation protocol on Quantinuum’s system model H1 trapped-ion quantum processor, and use it to fault-tolerantly implement and benchmark a logical non-Clifford gate, a controlled-Hadamard (CH), with significantly lower error than the physical CH gate.

results.finding: Neutral-atom logical processor: up to 448 atoms; universal logical rotations demonstrated with up to 3 T gates.
results.detail: The experiment used transversal logical CZ gates and teleportation to implement Hadamard and T operations on Reed–Muller code blocks. Logical feedforward was applied in software.

results.finding: Silicon donor processor with two logical qubits demonstrated a universal logical gate set.
results.detail: The logical CNOT and some single-qubit gates were fault-tolerant, but the implemented S gate was non-fault-tolerant. The T gate was evaluated by postselecting an ancilla outcome; mid-circuit measurements were unavailable.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate a logical quantum processor based on the [[4, 2, 2]] code using five nuclear spins in a silicon donor system

results.finding: An 8-qubit superconducting experiment achieved a 9.6 μs full decoding response time.
results.detail: The decoder operated after the measurement rounds, rather than in streaming mode. Its result triggered a conditional physical gate; a dependent logical gate was not demonstrated. Mean decoding time per round was below the syndrome production interval, providing evidence for future streaming throughput.
results.quote: We present a real-time decoded QEC experiment on 8 qubits with logical branching that measures the full decoding response time to be 9.6 μs, including 6.5 μs decoding time and 3.1 μs communication and control latency times, per 9 measurement rounds.

results.finding: A decoder for a 17-qubit superconducting surface code achieved 550 ns closed-loop feedback latency.
results.detail: The decoder’s 184 ns throughput period was shorter than the 1.25 μs QEC cycle. Feedback preceded non-Clifford logical rotations; that demonstration used a simplified non-fault-tolerant protocol and post-selection.
results.quote: The system achieves a deterministic closed-loop latency of 550 ns, including 124 ns for NN decoding, enabling feedback corrections within a 1.25 us QEC cycle.

results.finding: On 30 trapped-ion qubits, the 1QEC teleportation circuit used real-time decoding four times.
results.detail: A lookup-table decoder processed syndromes and active corrections were applied before the Bell measurement. The source does not report decoder throughput or response latency, or establish that backlog is avoided during repeated correction cycles.
results.quote: For clarity, we emphasize that real-time decoding occurs four times in this circuit. During the QEC gadget and the three destructive logical measurements, the decoder measures syndromes and determines corrections.

results.finding: Aurora decoded two repetition-code checks and used the result to select a measurement basis at time step 5.
results.detail: The integrated decoder supplied real-time feedforward for an error-detection experiment, but the text does not establish sustained syndrome-processing throughput or corrections before dependent logical gates.
